In words with the following vowel configurations two stress patterns are possible: [table: 1 final e after i, e, a: píre ~ piré 'wolf' ...; 4 final ə after i, e, a, ö, ü, o, u: kítšəm ~ kitšə́m 'his hand (acc.)' ...; 5 final e, ö, o, ə after ə: púgəlmö ~ pügəlmö́ 'cone' ...] In such words, stress may fall on either the final vowel — although a few final morphemes, such as -kən 'if,' never carry stress — or on the nearest preceding “full” vowel. sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title, Lehiste et al. 2005 'Meadow Mari Prosody' (Glottolog 110928), already held with a text layer from the 2026-09-16 download (kirj.ee open PDF, DOI 10.3176/lu.2005.2s); re-read pp.13-14, 17-30, 64-71, 91-94 and logged in It is squarely about word stress in this language (Meadow = Eastern Mari, mhr) and REFINES the catalog's weight-hedged coding: the received rule 'last full vowel, else initial' appears only as the reported common claim (p.14, quoting Kangasmaa-Minn 1998:224 verbatim on p.20; Itkonen/Kiparsky on p.21), while the authors' own 8-speaker acoustic data show placement is not fixed (speakers disagreed on 16/58 disyllables and 7/17 trisyllables; a Bashkortostan speaker favoured initial stress), at least one stress minimal pair exists (šérge 'dear' ~ šergé 'comb'), duration is the main cue, and all-schwa words are initially stressed (pp.64-65, 68-69, 93-94). This contradicts Sebeok & Ingemann 1961's 'stress is not phonemic' assumption in the deciding quote but not the coded rule; it is the best first-hand support for the 'hedged' flag rather than a replacement deciding source for the placement rule (Kangasmaa-Minn 1998 / Riese et al. 2022 / Vaysman 2009, already in the record, remain the rule statements). Chapter 2 also supplies verified verbatim secondary quotes (Collinder 1965:42-43, Ristinen 1960:259, Karmazin 1936, Zorina 1982:46, Kuklin 2003) usable in the bibliography. Nothing left to acquire for this item

new_statements.quote: Stress position appears not to be fixed with reference to a given syllable within a word. For example, in the set of disyllabic words, there were 29 words where the speakers stressed the first syllable, 13 words with stress on the second syllable, and in the case of 16 words, different speakers positioned stress differently. [p.64] ... One of the identificational characteristics of words containing exclusively central vowels is the localization of stress on the first syllable. [p.94]

new_statements.reading: First-hand instrumental evidence from 8 speakers that Meadow Mari word stress is lexically variable rather than positionally fixed, with real inter- and intra-speaker disagreement, that it can be contrastive (one minimal pair), and that all-reduced-vowel words take initial stress. It supports the weight basis (full vs reduced vowel) and, strongly, the 'hedged' flag; it does not itself state the 'last full vowel, else initial' rule from its own data but reports it as the received claim (Kangasmaa-Minn 1998:224, quoted verbatim on p.20).

sources.note: Eight-speaker acoustic study (100 test words x 2 frame positions = 1600 tokens) of Standard Meadow Mari. Its own data: stress is not fixed to a syllable; placement varied between speakers in 16 of 58 disyllables and 7 of 17 trisyllables, and the same speaker could shift stress between frames (p.64-65, 69); speaker LV, a native of Bashkortostan (the Eastern-dialect area proper), tended to stress first syllables more than the others (p.65). Duration is the reliable stress cue, F0 auxiliary and overridden by sentence intonation, unstressed vowels reduce (pp.71, 92-93). At least one minimal pair…
